headline: Terns Tight on the Rocks at Horton Point — Bluefish Behind Them, Bass Still Waiting
subhead: Bunker pushed into the beach this week woke up the blues while stripers hang back for cooler water and a bigger moon.
body_markdown:
Ray Tuthill's been tending the same string of oyster cages off Mattituck Inlet for going on thirty years, and he's got one rule he trusts more than any weather app: when the terns quit working the open water and start diving tight against the rocks, something's pushed the bait shallow. He called the bait shop Tuesday to report the birds were stacked up hard against Horton Point, working low and fast over the boulders. That's about as reliable a forecast as this stretch of Sound gives you, and it turned out right — a run of bunker got pinned against the beach there by midweek, and the bluefish showed up behind them like they'd been invited.

That's the story for the North Fork's Sound side this week: bluefish carrying the load, porgy holding steady as the sure thing, fluke thinning out the way it always does this time of year, and striped bass sitting on the sideline waiting for a signal that hasn't quite come yet. The water tells part of it. Kings Point over on the west end of the Sound is reading close to 71 degrees, New London down near the Race is running about 69.4, and that gradient runs right through this beat — warmer water piling up toward Mattituck, a cooler bite of it working in from Plum Gut east. Bass don't love either extreme this time of year. They want the bait concentrated, and the bait isn't quite there yet.

Bluefish don't share that problem. They've been the most dependable predator on this stretch straight through the month, tracking bunker schools that have been moving in pods along the beach from Mattituck to Rocky Point. When those schools get pinned against structure — a rock pile, a point, a current seam — the blues pile in and it turns into fast fishing for twenty minutes at a stretch. Diamond jigs in the one-to-two-ounce range worked with a fast retrieve have been doing the damage, and so have bunker chunks fished on wire leader for anyone who'd rather sit and let the current do the work. We flagged a couple weeks back that bluefish activity would track bunker density, and that's exactly the pattern playing out now — where the bunker balls are thick, the blues are thick behind them, and where the bait's thinned, so has the bite.

Porgy fishing remains the fallback that never seems to fail this time of year, and it hasn't changed. The rock piles off Horton Point and the drop-offs east of Rocky Point are holding good numbers of scup in the eight-to-twelve-inch class, with a scattering of better fish mixed in on the deeper structure. Small hooks, sandworms or squid strips, light sinkers — nothing complicated about it, and it's about the only bite around here you can set a watch by right now.

Fluke have gone soft, which is normal for the end of August and nothing to read too much into. The warm water sitting up in the shallows has pushed them out toward the inlets and deeper channel edges where there's a bit more oxygen and a bit less heat. Mattituck Inlet itself has been giving up a few keeper-class fish to white Gulp paired with a half-ounce bucktail, worked slow along the channel drop on the last of the outgoing. It's not the kind of fishing that fills a cooler fast, but patient anglers working the deeper edges are still connecting. We said this stretch would hold catchable fluke into September before the offshore push starts in earnest, and that's holding true — just don't expect the June numbers.

Striped bass are the one everybody's watching and nobody's catching much of yet. There's fish around — a few taken on bunker chunks at first light off Rocky Point, a handful more on eels worked slow through the Plum Gut approach on a strong tide stage — but it's spotty, not a pattern you can plan a trip around. The real trigger is bait density, and right now the bunker schools that will eventually pull bass into blitz mode are still scattered rather than balled up tight. That tends to change fast once the moon builds toward full and the tides start moving more water — probably another week to two weeks out, based on how this has gone in past seasons. When it turns, it usually turns quick, and Plum Gut is the place to be watching, since that's where the first pushes of bait and predator alike tend to funnel through on a strong tide.

Speaking of Plum Gut — keep an eye out there for something besides bass. There's bonito working the Race and the Rhode Island side of the Sound already, and this stretch sits close enough to catch the overflow if that push keeps drifting west. Nothing confirmed on this side yet, but small metal jigs and epoxy flies would be the play if they show.

Blackfish remain off the table, and that's no surprise — we said last week the bigger tautog story here is still weeks off, waiting on the Sound to cool down further, and nothing this week changes that read. For now, work the bunker-and-tern pattern for blues, hit the rock piles for a reliable bag of porgy, and if you want fluke, fish the channel edges slow rather than the flats. The next real shift on this beat is the bass turning on with the bigger tides — watch the moon, watch the bait, and watch Plum Gut closest of all.
